claims.text: The starting coating is a nanoscale multilayer composed of chemically complex high-entropy alloys containing both FCC and BCC phases.
The starting material exhibits severe lattice distortion.
The starting material has local chemical short-range order.
Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading is primarily governed by strain-induced formation of localized amorphous bands at nanoscale interfaces.
Localized amorphous regions redistribute interfacial stress.
Localized amorphous regions delay abrupt dislocation glide.
Stress redistribution and delayed dislocation glide enable a balance between high strength and deformation tolerance.
Sustained creep-like loading while preserving the layered architecture is the proposed intervention.
Localized amorphous bands form preferentially at multilayer interfaces and possibly near grain boundaries because of concentrated strain and defect reorganization.
Severe lattice distortion and chemical short-range order impede long-range conventional dislocation glide in high-entropy alloys.
Impeded dislocation glide causes sustained loading to concentrate stress in interfacial regions.
Once a critical local stress is reached, dislocation interactions and stacking-fault reorganization trigger an amorphous transformation.
The resulting amorphous bands act as gradient mediators for plastic flow and progressively accommodate strain without catastrophic failure.
Sustained strain training will gradually increase the fraction of amorphous material along the interfaces relative to the baseline.
Increasing interfacial amorphization will produce smoother and more homogeneous plastic flow, fewer stress serrations, and a moderated creep rate.
The proposed baseline deforms predominantly through conventional dislocation slip with abrupt stress drops and without significant amorphization.
The proposed mechanism applies only while nanoscale layering and substantial crystalline order are retained and catastrophic shear banding is avoided.
Prior studies in similar deformation-tolerant alloys have demonstrated strain-induced amorphization.
Periodic interruption and quenching followed by TEM, diffraction mapping, and mechanical measurements can test whether interfacial amorphization evolves concurrently with creep deformation.

The hypothesis is falsified if sustained loading causes no significant increase in localized interfacial amorphous regions and deformation remains solely dislocation-mediated without a gradient-mediated transition.
